=== Shell Energy Comments 58777 Staff Questions on Study Assumptions.pdf ===
                                         PROJECT NO. 58777

        TRIENNIAL RELIABILITY                         §    PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
      ASSESSMENT FOR THE ERCOT                        §
         REGION UNDER §25.508                         §                  OF TEXAS
                                                      §


        SHELL ENERGY’S RESPONSE TO QUESTIONS ON ERCOT'S PROPOSED
             ASSUMPTIONS FOR THE 2026 RELIABILITY ASSESSMENT

         Shell Energy North America (US) LP (“Shell Energy”) respectfully submits these comments
in response to questions posed by the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) Staff
(“Staff”) regarding the 2026 Reliability Assessment assumptions proposed by the Electrical Reliability
Council of Texas (“ERCOT”). Shell Energy participates broadly in the ERCOT market, spanning retail
electric service, thermal generation ownership, energy scheduling and dispatch, renewable and
emerging technology development, and risk management services. Given the wide array of
involvement, Shell Energy advocates for transparent, competitive, technology-neutral market-based
solutions which can achieve the desired reliability objectives in near and long term horizons at the
lowest cost to consumers.
         Shell Energy greatly appreciates the Commission and Staff’s continued attention to this
critically important matter and is grateful for the opportunity to provide input on the questions at issue.
Shell Energy looks forward to continued collaboration with the Commission and ERCOT as this
important work progresses.
                                         I.      COMMENTS

         Shell Energy passionately believes that the credibility and viability of the triennial assessment
depends fundamentally on the accuracy, transparency, and analytical rigor of the underlying
assumptions. The objective of the assessment should be the development of accurate, evidence-based
projections rather than develop projections based on conservative assumptions that inadvertently
distort system conditions. Sensitivities can provide wider range of potential outcomes in this highly
variable environment, but the core of the project must be focused on accuracy to support informed
decision-making by policymakers, investors, and market participants. Without confidence in the
results, no real investment decision can be made by market participants and no lasting market design
change decisions can be made by regulators. If there is no agreement on the magnitude and longevity
of the impacts by developers and financial institutions, then long-term investments in ERCOT will
still be limited.

         The most important and impactful input into this assessment is the load forecast. The use of an
inflated forecast will decimate any veracity in decisions made based on this assessment. Particularly,
the way large loads are considered in the load projections is concerning, and it is evident that a more
accurate forecast is necessary. This is evident in prior reactions to the forecast in the forward markets,
initially there was a spike based on the high load projection, but the prices quickly normalized after
skepticism in the projections grew. The uncertainty in the load forecast is the biggest factor dampening
 investment signals. The Capacity, Demand, and Reserves (CDR) report used to move the market
heavily, but conservative assumptions and practices have led investors to lose faith in its results, which
now have little to no impact on forward markets. Given the Panda Power1 history where reliance on
an overstated forecast led to financial distress, the market needs much more certainty on the projections
to make investment decisions. Senate Bill 6 (“SB6”) criteria should be applied even if that will
introduce a bit of delay in timeline. Similarly, if the regulators intend to attract investments in thermal
resources, then a realistic Cost of New Entry (“CONE”) value should be used even if it takes time to
update the values.

         Shell Energy is concerned that the conservative selection of parameters, such as the
effectiveness of weatherization efforts, would produce extreme results which, when compounded with
other assumptions, would diminish the assessment’s credibility. Another highly impactful parameter
is the perceived probability of extreme weather events. A weather year probability should be made to
reflect its likelihood of reoccurrence and not be skewed by the limited sample size or recency bias in
the underlying data. It is important to use the actual probability of extreme events instead of assuming
equal probability or recency bias, which would inflate Uri from a 1 in 100 event to 1 in 44 or 1 in 26,
respectively, overstating risk. Even if equal probability and recency bias is applied for generic years,
extreme event’s probability should be updated to reflect its actual likelihood of reoccurrence.

                                  II. RESPONSE TO STAFF QUESTIONS

1) At the July 25, 2024 open meeting, the Commission approved setting the CONE at
   $140,000/MW-year for planning purposes in the ERCOT region, including the triennial
   reliability assessment. Based on stakeholder feedback, ERCOT has proposed a plan for
   updating this CONE value.
    a. Does CONE need to be updated for the 2026 reliability standard assessment? Why or
        why not?
    b. If the Commission considers an updated CONE value, are the scope and list of tasks
        proposed by Brattle and Sargent & Lundy in ERCOT’s January 15, 2026 filing an
        acceptable method to update the calculations? If not, please provide recommended
        modifications to their approach.

        Updating the Cost of New Entry (“CONE”) for use in the 2026 reliability assessment is
essential to ensure that the study reflects realistic market conditions and produces outcomes that
meaningfully inform Commission decision-making. The currently approved CONE value of
$140,000/MW-year is substantially below the cost of developing new thermal generation resources
and therefore does not provide a credible basis for evaluating the magnitude of market signals required
to attract new dispatchable capacity.

       If the Commission were to rely on an understated CONE value, any resulting market reforms
could fail to elicit new investment in reliable, flexible, dispatchable resources. At the approved level
of $140,000/MW-year, the development of new thermal generation would be challenging absent

1
 See Panda Power Generation Infrastructure Fund, LLC d/b/a Panda Power Funds, et al. v. Electric Reliability Council
of Texas, Inc., Cause No. CV-16-0401, 15th Dist. Ct., Grayson County, Tex. (filed Feb. 29, 2016).
 substantial out-of-market support, and the inadequacy of this signal could jeopardize effective price
formation and increase the risk of premature retirements of existing resources that must continue to
make substantial capital investments to maintain reliability.

       For these reasons, Shell Energy recommends that the Commission update the CONE value for
the 2026 assessment to ensure that the analysis reflects realistic investment costs and provides
policymakers with an accurate understanding of the market reforms needed to support development
of new dispatchable generation.

2) ERCOT has requested the Commission consider whether the load forecasts used in this
   study should align with the one that will be generated through the 2026 RTP compliance
   plan described in the Commission’s rulemaking in Project No. 58480. ERCOT
   acknowledges that an updated load forecast that aligns with that compliance plan could be
   ready by April or May 2026, which would push back the timeline of the reliability
   assessment by at least a month.
   a. Should the Commission approve updating the load forecast used in the 2026 reliability
      assessment to align with the compliance plan being considered in Project No. 58480,
      even if it will delay work on the reliability assessment?
   b. What other considerations should the Commission make regarding the load forecast
      used for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years?

        It is essential that the Commission require the 2026 reliability assessment to incorporate the
most accurate load forecast available, even if doing so results in a modest delay to the study timeline.
Industry stakeholders universally agree that requiring greater financial commitment from prospective
large loads significantly improves forecast accuracy and more appropriately assigns risk away from
consumers. Ensuring alignment with the criteria under development in Project No. 58480, without
grandfathering previously included loads, will strengthen the credibility of the resulting projections
and enhance the reliability of any conclusions drawn from the assessment. A one-month delay is a
reasonable and necessary tradeoff to ensure that the Commission has confidence in the study’s output.

         ERCOT should also closely examine the load levels used in each simulation to ensure they are
realistic and supported by empirical evidence. ERCOT’s preliminary presentations indicate that
several weather years produce winter 2026 net loads exceeding 90 GW, with the potential for
additional upward adjustments from other study factors. These levels are not credible and would
artificially inflate the projected magnitude and frequency of load shed events. A reasonable upper
bound on load levels should be considered to prevent unrealistic assumptions from distorting results.
         ERCOT’s previous analyses demonstrate that the likelihood of a 4% upward load-forecast error
is extremely low, and because threshold calculations do not consider probabilities, care should be taken
in the inclusion of these cases to avoid skewing magnitude and duration calculations. It begs the
questions whether upward load-forecast error should be applied to extreme cases at all. The precise
2021 load, excluding firm load shed, remains unknown, and ERCOT’s estimate appears to be
overstated. Incorporating non-weather-related load forecast errors would further distort upwards
already exaggerated winter storm Uri load data and significantly skew the results.
         Furthermore, it is important to ensure that the duplicate cases introduced for 2021 and 1989 to
add additional risk in January do not result in double counting scenarios when evaluating magnitude
and duration tolerances. The ERCOT filing indicates that probabilities are re-weighted for these
additional cases, which effectively addresses the double counting concern in the 1-in-10 LOLE
analysis. However, duplicity remains an issue in compliance processes such as threshold checks for
magnitude and duration, as these procedures do not apply weighting. Incorporating duplicate year
scenarios alters the empirical distribution of cases. Unless the duplicates are excluded from magnitude
and duration calculations, the results, specifically the largest non-excluded case, will be significantly
skewed upward. This occurs for two primary reasons: (1) magnitude and duration metrics use the
empirical 99th percentile order statistic across all scenarios rather than probability-weighted values;
and (2) the two additional profiles represent severe winter conditions and disproportionately affect the
upper tail, leading to doubled extreme violation cases. While increasing the total number of cases also
raises the number trimmed by the 1% threshold, the doubling of extreme violation cases due to these
profiles negates any mitigation of bias in the underlying scenarios.
3) ERCOT proposed using the December 2025 Capacity, Demand, and Reserves (CDR)
   Report to create the base portfolio for evaluating the bulk power system in 2026 and 2029.
   This includes resource additions and retirements.
   a. Does the generation portfolio in the December 2025 CDR Report adequately capture
      the resource mix in both 2026 and 2029? If not, what additional assumptions should be
      made about resource additions and retirements?

        Using the generation portfolio from the December 2025 CDR Report is a reasonable approach
for establishing the 2026 study year, as the set of potential resource additions and retirements within
that timeframe is relatively well understood. In contrast, applying the same methodology to the 2029
study year is inappropriate given the significantly greater uncertainty associated with the longer
planning horizon and the higher-risk load forecast that will be used for that period.

        For the 2029 portfolio, ERCOT should, at a minimum, include all generation resources
identified in the Texas Energy Fund (“TEF”), incorporate additional projects that are likely to meet
inclusion criteria before 2029, and re-evaluate any assumed retirements to ensure they reflect realistic
expectations rather than conservative assumptions. The extensive stakeholder discussions during
Planning Guide Revision Request (“PGRR”) 127, which refined the criteria for including resources in
transmission planning cases, provide an appropriate and structured framework that ERCOT should
leverage when determining the 2029 resource mix. Delaying proposed retirements and incorporating
additional generation that is reasonably anticipated, even if not yet fully qualified under the stringent
CDR criteria, would produce a more balanced and analytically sound portfolio, particularly given that
the load forecast being introduced into the assessment has a far less rigorous standard.

4) Based on information provided by the transmission operators, ERCOT proposed using
   13,988 MW as the magnitude criterion of the reliability standard for the 2026 simulation
   year. For the 2029 simulation year, ERCOT proposes scaling the 2026 magnitude value by
   the ratio of the 75th percentile load forecast for 2029 to the 75th percentile load forecast for
   2026, resulting in a magnitude value of 14,509 MW for the 2029 simulation year.
     a. Should the Commission use these values for the magnitude criterion in the 2026 and
       2029 simulation years? If not, what modifications to these values should be made?

         ERCOT’s proposed magnitude criteria, 13,988 MW for 2026 and 14,509 MW for 2029, are
derived from low-percentile load forecasts that do not align with the system conditions under which
reliability events are expected to occur. The study’s preliminary results indicate that load shed events
predominantly arise under high-percentile conditions, with winter 2026 net loads frequently exceeding
90 GW. As a result, applying magnitude thresholds based on 77–80 GW load levels significantly
understates the amount of load that must be rollable to maintain service during extreme conditions.
Scaling ERCOT’s methodology to more realistic load levels when load shed will occur suggests a
magnitude threshold closer to 16 GW, even before accounting for additional conservative assumptions
in the study.

        It appears that ERCOT estimated the system’s total shed load by using the percentage of load
rotation possible for the most limited TDSP, then applying that same percentage across all TDSPs.
However, a more accurate approach would be to determine what proportion of load each TDSP can
actually shed and sum those amounts to find the systemwide total. If assigning different load shed
percentages to individual TDSPs proves challenging, at minimum, larger TDSPs should be assigned
higher percentages.

        In addition, ERCOT’s methodology assumes rotation between only two load-shed groups,
resulting in an effective rollable load of approximately 14 GW at any given time—implying 28 GW
of load located on curtailable circuits. Increasing the number of rotational groups to three or four, as
several transmission and distribution service providers have indicated, could be feasible with targeted
system improvements, would meaningfully expand the volume of load that can be rotated without
sustaining prolonged outages. Under a three-group rotation scheme, approximately 18.7 GW could
remain offline at any given time, increasing to roughly 21 GW under a four-group rotation.
       Moreover, ERCOT should indicate, for each simulation, the scaled level of rollable load and
whether the load shed in that scenario would have been fully rollable under realistic operational
conditions. Providing this information alongside the traditional magnitude comparison would give
Commissioners a more complete understanding of system performance under extreme conditions.

        Finally, consistent with Senate Bill 6, large loads are required to be curtailed prior to firm load
shed. This program should be treated as an available resource within the reliability assessment and
reflected in determinations of whether the magnitude criterion has been exceeded. Large loads should
therefore be considered fully curtailable for purposes of reducing unserved energy, rather than included
in the calculation of firm-load magnitude violations.

5) ERCOT proposed using the EIA’s 2025 Annual Energy Outlook and EIA Form 923 data to
   determine the natural gas and coal prices for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years. This
   results in prices of $2.84/MMBtu for natural gas and $2.47/MMBtu for coal in 2026 and
   $3.16/MMBtu for natural gas and $2.41/MMBtu for coal in 2029.
     a. Are these assumptions for fuel prices for the 2026/2029 simulation years reasonable? If
       not, what alternative sources of information should be considered to determine these
       fuels prices?
    b. Should any sensitivity analyses on these fuel prices be considered?
        ERCOT’s proposal to rely on the fuel-price assumptions derived from the EIA’s 2025 Annual
Energy Outlook and EIA Form 923 provides a reasonable foundation for establishing natural gas and
coal prices for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years. However, given the uncertainty inherent in
long-term commodity price forecasting and the material influence fuel prices can have on dispatch
outcomes and system reliability modeling, it would be prudent for the Commission to require a
sensitivity analysis that evaluates a reasonable range of alternative fuel-price assumptions.

        Conducting such a sensitivity analysis would help ensure that the results of the reliability
assessment are not unduly dependent on any single fuel-price trajectory. It would also provide market
participants and policymakers with a clearer understanding of how variations in natural gas and coal
prices may affect the frequency, magnitude, and duration of loss-of-load events. Incorporating these
sensitivities would strengthen the robustness of the assessment and enhance confidence in the study’s
conclusion.

6) For previous reliability assessments, ERCOT has treated all historical weather years as
   having equal probability. For this assessment, ERCOT proposed weighing recent years more
   heavily.
    a. Should the Commission consider not treating all historical weather years as having
       equal probability? If yes, do you agree with ERCOT’s proposed weighting of weather
       years?
    b. If you have an alternative weighting methodology, please provide additional details on
       your proposal. Please include justification for why your approach is better than what
       ERCOT has proposed.

        ERCOT’s proposal to apply recency weighting to historical weather years warrants careful
reconsideration. While incorporating recency may appear reasonable at a conceptual level, doing so
will significantly overstate the probability of recent extreme events. Under ERCOT’s approach, the
modeled probability of Winter Storm Uri is increased from an already elevated 2.27% to 3.84%,
effectively treating Uri as a one-in-twenty-six-year event, despite its widely recognized return interval
of one in one hundred to one in two hundred years. Such an inflation of risk is inconsistent with
climatological evidence and introduces substantial bias into the reliability assessment. While equal
probability and recency bias may be appropriate for generic years, extreme events require distinct
consideration. Their probabilities should be recalibrated to accurately reflect their true likelihood of
recurrence.

         ERCOT and the Commission have previously completed extensive work in Project No. 52691
to analyze historical probabilities of weather patterns, and this analysis should be leveraged to assign
probability weights that reflect realistic likelihoods of reoccurrence. Because PowerGEM has
indicated that adjusting weather-year probabilities is operationally trivial and would not delay study
results, ERCOT should calibrate the probability of Uri to a level consistent with its expected frequency.
 At a minimum, the Commission should require a sensitivity case that applies more realistic probability
assumptions to ensure that policymakers are not relying on overstated extreme-event risks.

        Finally, if ERCOT elects to incorporate recency bias, it is unclear why weather years 2024 and
2025 have been omitted. ERCOT has indicated that portions of 2025 data may have availability
constraints; however, 2024 data is fully available and should be included to maintain methodological
consistency. Partial inclusion of 2025 data should also be considered if it is available as well.

7) ERCOT proposed using the multi-area reliability and economic dispatch modeling
   capability in SERVM to assess resource adequacy on a zonal basis that would account for
   transmission constraints between defined transmission zones. ERCOT states that any
   results from this analysis would be informational and not used to determine compliance
   with the reliability standard.
    a. Should the Commission approve an assessment of reliability metrics at the zonal level,
       understanding that these results would be purely informational and not used to
       determine compliance with the reliability standard?
    b. If so, do you have any proposed modifications to the approach ERCOT has
       recommended?

        ERCOT’s proposal to conduct a zonal-level reliability assessment using the multiarea
modeling capabilities within SERVM may offer supplemental insight, but its application in this context
must be carefully qualified. The zonal analysis relies on dispatch assumptions and outage probabilities
that reflect average system conditions, which differ materially from the conditions present during
extreme events—the primary focus of this assessment. As a result, any zonal-level outputs would have
limited relevance to evaluating system performance under the high-stress reliability scenarios that
drive the Commission’s reliability standard.

       Given these limitations, any zonal results should be explicitly characterized as informational
and should not be used for compliance purposes or interpreted as producing deterministic conclusions
regarding system adequacy. Moreover, several issues explored within this zonal construct are more
appropriately addressed through the ongoing Regional Transmission Plan (“RTP”) process, rather than
through a resource-adequacy assessment designed to evaluate loss-of-load risk under extreme
conditions.

8) ERCOT proposed modifying how the model accounts for the effectiveness of the
   Commission’s weatherization rule 16 TAC § 25.55. Previously, it was estimated to reduce
   weather-related outages by 85%, however under ERCOT’s proposed approach, the rule’s
   effectiveness would decline during extreme temperatures.
    a. Do you agree with ERCOT’s recommendation to deviate from the 85% effectiveness for
        the weatherization rule?

       Decreasing the assumed effectiveness of weatherization measures for temperatures below the
Commission-established standard may be reasonable in principle; however, the rate of degradation
proposed by ERCOT is excessively severe and unsupported by recent operational evidence. ERCOT’s
methodology suggests that under conditions comparable to Winter Storm Uri, the substantial
 weatherization investments made over the past five years would provide no meaningful benefit,
despite extensive improvements across the generating fleet. This assumption is inconsistent with
observed generator performance and therefore lacks analytical justification.

        Recent weather events further demonstrate that ERCOT’s proposed base line of only 85%
reduction of weather-related outages and erosion curve significantly understates generator capability.
During Winter Storm Fern, many areas experienced wind-chill conditions more than 10 degrees below
the weatherization standard without any correlated deterioration in weatherization effectiveness, and
most generators continued to operate reliably well below the required threshold. These data points
directly contradict the premise that benefits should disappear within a 15-degree temperature
differential.

        Given the magnitude of the potential impacts, adjusting this assumption is critically important.
ERCOT’s initial trial analysis indicates that reducing weatherization effectiveness in the manner
proposed would nearly double the projected Loss of Load Expectation and magnitude in the 2026
assessment, with even more pronounced effects anticipated in the higher-load 2029 study year. Such
distortions would materially diminish the reliability and credibility of the study results.

        Accordingly, ERCOT should modify its baseline to incorporate evidence of overperformance
in the past storms and the proposed erosion curve methodology should either be removed or
significantly modified to reflect a more realistic, gradual decline in effectiveness, one that is consistent
with empirical performance data and the substantial weatherization efforts undertaken by the
generation community.

9) ERCOT has proposed assumptions for the outages:
    a. Are the assumptions for generation and ESR outage modeling reasonable? If not, what
       modifications do you propose?
    b. How should ERCOT treat planned transmission outages in the model?

        Transmission outages could only be taken into consideration in the zonal analysis and as
stated above that has limited value.
10) Please provide comments and recommendations on any of the model input assumptions that
    Staff has not specifically flagged in previous questions.

        ERCOT’s analysis of load-forecast error in the 2025 Ancillary Services (AS) methodology
found that historical load growth exhibited weak or inconsistent relationships with forecast-error
magnitudes, and therefore error inputs were not scaled with load levels. In contrast, the current study
applies fixed percentage error values, 0%, 2%, and 4%, which necessarily scale with total load and
disproportionately affect extreme-weather scenarios. This approach is inconsistent with ERCOT’s
prior findings and results in an inflated representation of uncertainty, particularly given that the
underlying load forecast is already subject to considerable variability and appears likely to be
overstated in magnitude.
       Moreover, while forecast uncertainty may reasonably increase for later years, the assessment
does not apply a comparable uncertainty range to resource additions, creating an analytical imbalance
 between load- and supply-side assumptions. To maintain consistency and avoid compounding
conservatism, ERCOT should refrain from applying non-weather-based load-forecast error for the
2029 study year or, at a minimum, should employ the 2026 error probabilities instead.

        When conducting long-term projections of this nature, uncertainty is unavoidable. Providing a
broader range of scenarios and sensitivities, similar to the approach used in the CDR report, would
offer the Commission a more complete picture of potential outcomes. Additional efforts examining
adjustments to Ancillary Service Demand Curves (“ASDC”s) and increases to the system-wide offer
cap would further support evaluation of market-design options intended to incentivize the
development of additional dispatchable generation.

III.   Conclusion

        Shell Energy appreciates the Commission’s thoughtful engagement on the assumptions guiding
the 2026 Reliability Assessment and welcomes the opportunity to contribute to this important process.
Ensuring that the study’s inputs are accurate, transparent, and reflective of realistic system conditions
is essential to producing results that can meaningfully inform long-term market design and policy
decisions. Shell Energy respectfully submits the recommendations provided herein to support a more
credible, analytically sound assessment, and one that provides policymakers with the clarity necessary
to evaluate reliability outcomes and prioritize future market design considerations.

        Shell Energy remains fully available to discuss these comments in greater detail and to support
Staff or Commissioners with any additional analysis, clarification, or follow-up that may assist in the
development of a robust and reliable final assessment.


                                              Respectfully submitted,

                                              Shane Thomas
                                              Director, Regulatory Policy

                                                 IV.     Executive Summary
1. The reliability assessment must be grounded in accurate, evidence-based assumptions.
    Load credibility of the study depends on inputs that reflect realistic system conditions rather than conservative
    assumptions that inflate risk or distort outcomes.
2. An updated load forecast is essential to maintaining analytical integrity.
    The ERCOT’s current forecasts produce implausibly high net-load levels, such as winter 2026 net loads
    exceeding 90 GW, which artificially increase modeled load-shed events. Aligning the assessment with the criteria
    in Project No. 58480, without grandfathering prior inclusions, is necessary even if it delays the study by a month.
3. The Cost of New Entry (CONE) must be updated to reflect actual development costs.
    The approved value of $140,000/MW-year is materially understated relative to the cost of new thermal resources.
    If retained, it would fail to reflect needed realistic investment signals, impede development of new dispatchable
    generation, and risk premature retirements.
4. Weatherization-effectiveness assumptions must reflect empirical performance.
    ERCOT should modify its baseline to incorporate evidence of overperformance in the past storms. ERCOT’s
    proposed erosion curve eliminates weatherization benefits too quickly and should include a more gradual,
    evidence-based decline consistent with observed generator performance to avoid overstating loss-of-load risks.
5. Weather-year weighting must not inflate extreme-event probabilities.
    ERCOT’s methodology increases the modeled probability of Winter Storm Uri beyond its climatological range,
    biasing reliability results. More realistic probability assumptions should be used or at least studied as sensitivity
    for 2021 and 1989. Inclusion of 2024 and partial 2025 data is needed based on arguments for recency weighting.
6. Resource portfolio assumptions for 2029 must reflect heightened uncertainty.
    While the December 2025 CDR mix is reasonable for 2026, applying it to 2029 is inappropriate. ERCOT should
    include all Texas Energy Fund resources and apply PGRR127’s structured criteria to incorporate additional
    projects reasonably expected to enter service.
7. Magnitude thresholds must correspond to extreme-event conditions and based on all TDSP’s abilities.
    ERCOT’s proposed thresholds are based on moderate load and understate potential rotatable load. More realistic
    scaling indicates thresholds closer to 16 GW. Increasing the number of rotational groups from two to three or four
    would further expand feasible rotatable load. The total load shed should not be calculated by using the lowest load
    rotation percentage from all TDSPs. Larger classes of TDSPs should have higher percentages, at a minimum.
8. Load curtailment under SB 6 should be treated as available tools in magnitude and duration calculations.
    The objective of curtailment options in SB6 is to maintain reliability during extreme events and hence those loads
    should be treated as curtailable rather than firm in magnitude and duration calculations.
9. Duplicate cases for 2021 and 1989 must not skew magnitude and duration calculation.
    Including duplicate scenarios skews empirical distributions and inflates results unless duplicates are excluded.
    This happens because: (1) magnitude and duration metrics rely on the empirical 99th percentile without
    probability weighting; (2) the added severe winter profiles disproportionately impact extreme violation counts.
    While more cases increase the number trimmed by the 1% threshold, doubling extreme cases offsets any
    reduction in skewness.
10. Load-forecast error should not scale with total load.
    ERCOT’s prior analysis found no consistent relationship between load growth and forecast error, yet the current
    assessment applies percentage-based error rates that inflate uncertainty during extreme conditions.
11. Non-weather-based load-forecast error should not be applied to extreme years.
    The precise 2021 load, excluding firm load shed, remains unknown, and ERCOT’s estimate appears to be
    overstated. Incorporating non-weather-related load forecast errors would further distort upwards already
    exaggerated winter storm Uri load data and significantly skew the result.

         Shell Energy is concerned that the conservative selection of parameters, such as the
effectiveness ofweatherization efforts, would produce extreme results which, when compounded with
other assumptions, would diminish the assessment's credibility. Another highly impactful parameter
is the perceived probability of extreme weather events. A weather year probability should be made to
reflect its likelihood of reoccurrence and not be skewed by the limited sample size or recency bias in
the underlying data. It is important to use the actual probability of extreme events instead of assuming
equal probability or recency bias, which would inflate Uri from a 1 in 100 event to 1 in 44 or 1 in 26,
respectively, overstating risk. Even if equal probability and recency bias is applied for generic years,
extreme event's probability should be updated to reflect its actual likelihood of reoccurrence.

                                   II. RESPONSE TO STAFF OUESTIONS

1) At the July 25, 2024 open meeting, the Commission approved setting the CONE at
   $140,000/MW-year for planning purposes in the ERCOT region, including the triennial
   reliability assessment. Based on stakeholder feedback, ERCOT has proposed a plan for
   updating this CONE value.
    a. Does CONE need to be updated for the 2026 reliability standard assessment? Why or
        why not?
    b. If the Commission considers an updated CONE value, are the scope and list of tasks
        proposed by Brattle and Sargent & Lundy in ERCOT's January 15, 2026 filing an
        acceptable method to update the calculations? If not, please provide recommended
        modifications to their approach.

        Updating the Cost of New Entry ("CONF) for use in the 2026 reliability assessment is
essential to ensure that the study reflects realistic market conditions and produces outcomes that
meaningfully inform Commission decision-making. The currently approved CONE value of
$140,000/MW-year is substantially below the cost of developing new thermal generation resources
and therefore does not provide a credible basis for evaluating the magnitude of market signals required
to attract new dispatchable capacity.

       If the Commission were to rely on an understated CONF, value, any resulting market reforms
could fail to elicit new investment in reliable, flexible, dispatchable resources. At the approved level
of $140,000/MW-year, the development of new thermal generation would be challenging absent

1 See Panda Power Generation Infrastructure Fund, LLC d/b/a Panda Power Funds, et al. v. Electric Reliability Council
of Texas, Inc., Cause No. CV-16-0401, 15th Dist. Ct., Grayson County, Tex. (filed Feb. 29, 2016).
 substantial out-of-market support, and the inadequacy of this signal could jeopardize effective price
formation and increase the risk of premature retirements of existing resources that must continue to
make substantial capital investments to maintain reliability.

       For these reasons, Shell Energy recommends that the Commission update the CONE value for
the 2026 assessment to ensure that the analysis reflects realistic investment costs and provides
policymakers with an accurate understanding of the market reforms needed to support development
of new dispatchable generation.

2) ERCOT has requested the Commission consider whether the load forecasts used in this
   study should align with the one that will be generated through the 2026 RTP compliance
   plan described in the Commission's rulemaking in Project No. 58480. ERCOT
   acknowledges that an updated load forecast that aligns with that compliance plan could be
   ready by April or May 2026, which would push back the timeline of the reliability
   assessment by at least a month.
   a. Should the Commission approve updating the load forecast used in the 2026 reliability
      assessment to align with the compliance plan being considered in Project No. 58480,
      even if it will delay work on the reliability assessment?
   b. What other considerations should the Commission make regarding the load forecast
      used for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years?

        It is essential that the Commission require the 2026 reliability assessment to incorporate the
most accurate load forecast available, even if doing so results in a modest delay to the study timeline.
Industry stakeholders universally agree that requiring greater financial commitment from prospective
large loads significantly improves forecast accuracy and more appropriately assigns risk away from
consumers. Ensuring alignment with the criteria under development in Project No. 58480, without
grandfathering previously included loads, will strengthen the credibility of the resulting proj ections
and enhance the reliability of any conclusions drawn from the assessment. A one-month delay is a
reasonable and necessary tradeoffto ensure that the Commission has confidence in the study's output.

         ERCOT should also closely examine the load levels used in each simulation to ensure they are
realistic and supported by empirical evidence. ERCOT's preliminary presentations indicate that
several weather years produce winter 2026 net loads exceeding 90 GW, with the potential for
additional upward adjustments from other study factors. These levels are not credible and would
artificially inflate the projected magnitude and frequency of load shed events. A reasonable upper
bound on load levels should be considered to prevent unrealistic assumptions from distorting results.
         ERCOT's previous analyses demonstrate that the likelihood of a 4% upward load-forecast error
is extremely low, and because threshold calculations do not consider probabilities, care should be taken
in the inclusion of these cases to avoid skewing magnitude and duration calculations. It begs the
questions whether upward load-forecast error should be applied to extreme cases at all. The precise
2021 load, excluding firm load shed, remains unknown, and ERCOT's estimate appears to be
overstated. Incorporating non-weather-related load forecast errors would further distort upwards
already exaggerated winter storm Uri load data and significantly skew the results.
        Furthermore, it is important to ensure that the duplicate cases introduced for 2021 and 1989 to
add additional risk in January do not result in double counting scenarios when evaluating magnitude
and duration tolerances. The ERCOT filing indicates that probabilities are re-weighted for these
additional cases, which effectively addresses the double counting concern in the 1-in-10 LOLE
analysis. However, duplicity remains an issue in compliance processes such as threshold checks for
magnitude and duration, as these procedures do not apply weighting. Incorporating duplicate year
scenarios alters the empirical distribution of cases. Unless the duplicates are excluded from magnitude
and duration calculations, the results, specifically the largest non-excluded case, will be significantly
skewed upward. This occurs for two primary reasons: (1) magnitude and duration metrics use the
empirical 99th percentile order statistic across all scenarios rather than probability-weighted values;
and (2) the two additional profiles represent severe winter conditions and disproportionately affect the
upper tail, leading to doubled extreme violation cases. While increasing the total number of cases also
raises the number trimmed by the 1% threshold, the doubling of extreme violation cases due to these
profiles negates any mitigation of bias in the underlying scenarios.

3) ERCOT proposed using the December 2025 Capacity, Demand, and Reserves (CDR)
   Report to create the base portfolio for evaluating the bulk power system in 2026 and 2029.
   This includes resource additions and retirements.
   a. Does the generation portfolio in the December 2025 CDR Report adequately capture
      the resource mix in both 2026 and 2029? If not, what additional assumptions should be
      made about resource additions and retirements?

       Using the generation portfolio from the December 2025 CDR Report is a reasonable approach
for establishing the 2026 study year, as the set of potential resource additions and retirements within
that timeframe is relatively well understood. In contrast, applying the same methodology to the 2029
study year is inappropriate given the significantly greater uncertainty associated with the longer
planning horizon and the higher-risk load forecast that will be used for that period.

        For the 2029 portfolio, ERCOT should, at a minimum, include all generation resources
identified in the Texas Energy Fund ("TEF"), incorporate additional projects that are likely to meet
inclusion criteria before 2029, and re-evaluate any assumed retirements to ensure they reflect realistic
expectations rather than conservative assumptions. The extensive stakeholder discussions during
Planning Guide Revision Request ("PGRR") 127, which refined the criteria for including resources in
transmission planning cases, provide an appropriate and structured framework that ERCOT should
leverage when determining the 2029 resource mix. Delaying proposed retirements and incorporating
additional generation that is reasonably anticipated, even if not yet fully qualified under the stringent
CDR criteria, would produce a more balanced and analytically sound portfolio, particularly given that
the load forecast being introduced into the assessment has a far less rigorous standard.

4) Based on information provided by the transmission operators, ERCOT proposed using
   13,988 MW as the magnitude criterion of the reliability standard for the 2026 simulation
   year. For the 2029 simulation year, ERCOT proposes scaling the 2026 magnitude value by
   the ratio of the 75th percentile load forecast for 2029 to the 75th percentile load forecast for
   2026, resulting in a magnitude value of 14,509 MW for the 2029 simulation year.
     a. Should the Commission use these values for the magnitude criterion in the 2026 and
       2029 simulation years? If not, what modifications to these values should be made?

       ERCOT's proposed magnitude criteria, 13,988 MW for 2026 and 14,509 MW for 2029, are
derived from low-percentile load forecasts that do not align with the system conditions under which
reliability events are expected to occur. The study's preliminary results indicate that load shed events
predominantly arise under high-percentile conditions, with winter 2026 net loads frequently exceeding
90 GW. As a result, applying magnitude thresholds based on 77-80 GW load levels significantly
understates the amount of load that must be rollable to maintain service during extreme conditions.
Scaling ERCOT's methodology to more realistic load levels when load shed will occur suggests a
magnitude threshold closer to 16 GW, even before accounting for additional conservative assumptions
in the study.

        It appears that ERCOT estimated the system's total shed load by using the percentage of load
rotation possible for the most limited TDSP, then applying that same percentage across all TDSPs.
However, a more accurate approach would be to determine what proportion of load each TDSP can
actually shed and sum those amounts to find the systemwide total. If assigning different load shed
percentages to individual TDSPs proves challenging, at minimum, larger TDSPs should be assigned
higher percentages.

        In addition, ERCOT's methodology assumes rotation between only two load-shed groups,
resulting in an effective rollable load of approximately 14 GW at any given time-implying 28 GW
of load located on curtailable circuits. Increasing the number of rotational groups to three or four, as
several transmission and distribution service providers have indicated, could be feasible with targeted
system improvements, would meaningfully expand the volume of load that can be rotated without
sustaining prolonged outages. Under a three-group rotation scheme, approximately 18.7 GW could
remain offline at any given time, increasing to roughly 21 GW under a four-group rotation.

       Moreover, ERCOT should indicate, for each simulation, the scaled level of rollable load and
whether the load shed in that scenario would have been fully rollable under realistic operational
conditions. Providing this information alongside the traditional magnitude comparison would give
Commissioners a more complete understanding of system performance under extreme conditions.

        Finally, consistent with Senate Bill 6, large loads are required to be curtailed prior to firm load
shed. This program should be treated as an available resource within the reliability assessment and
reflected in determinations of whether the magnitude criterion has been exceeded. Large loads should
therefore be considered fully curtailable for purposes of reducing unserved energy, rather than included
in the calculation of firm-load magnitude violations.

5) ERCOT proposed using the EIA's 2025 Annual Energy Outlook and EIA Form 923 data to
   determine the natural gas and coal prices for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years. This
   results in prices of $2.84/MMBtu for natural gas and $2.47/MMBtu for coal in 2026 and
   $3.16/MMBtu for natural gas and $2.41/MMBtu for coal in 2029.
     a. Are these assumptions for fuel prices for the 2026/2029 simulation years reasonable? If
       not, what alternative sources of information should be considered to determine these
       fuels prices?
    b. Should any sensitivity analyses on these fuel prices be considered?

        ERCOT's proposal to rely on the fuel-price assumptions derived from the EIA's 2025 Annual
Energy Outlook and EIA Form 923 provides a reasonable foundation for establishing natural gas and
coal prices for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years. However, given the uncertainty inherent in
long-term commodity price forecasting and the material influence fuel prices can have on dispatch
outcomes and system reliability modeling, it would be prudent for the Commission to require a
sensitivity analysis that evaluates a reasonable range of alternative fuel-price assumptions.

       Conducting such a sensitivity analysis would help ensure that the results of the reliability
assessment are not unduly dependent on any single fuel-price trajectory. It would also provide market
participants and policymakers with a clearer understanding of how variations in natural gas and coal
prices may affect the frequency, magnitude, and duration of loss-of-load events. Incorporating these
sensitivities would strengthen the robustness of the assessment and enhance confidence in the study's
conclusion.

6) For previous reliability assessments, ERCOT has treated all historical weather years as
   having equal probability. For this assessment, ERCOT proposed weighing recent years more
   heavily.
    a. Should the Commission consider not treating all historical weather years as having
       equal probability? If yes, do you agree with ERCOT's proposed weighting of weather
       years?
    b. If you have an alternative weighting methodology, please provide additional details on
       your proposal. Please include justification for why your approach is better than what
       ERCOT has proposed.

        ERCOT's proposal to apply recency weighting to historical weather years warrants careful
reconsideration. While incorporating recency may appear reasonable at a conceptual level, doing so
will significantly overstate the probability of recent extreme events. Under ERCOT's approach, the
modeled probability of Winter Storm Uri is increased from an already elevated 2.27% to 3.84%,
effectively treating Uri as a one-in-twenty-six-year event, despite its widely recognized return interval
of one in one hundred to one in two hundred years. Such an inflation of risk is inconsistent with
climatological evidence and introduces substantial bias into the reliability assessment. While equal
probability and recency bias may be appropriate for generic years, extreme events require distinct
consideration. Their probabilities should be recalibrated to accurately reflect their true likelihood of
recurrence.

         ERCOT and the Commission have previously completed extensive work in Project No. 52691
to analyze historical probabilities of weather patterns, and this analysis should be leveraged to assign
probability weights that reflect realistic likelihoods of reoccurrence. Because PowerGEM has
indicated that adjusting weather-year probabilities is operationally trivial and would not delay study
results, ERCOT should calibrate the probability of Uri to a level consistent with its expected frequency.
 At a minimum, the Commission should require a sensitivity case that applies more realistic probability
assumptions to ensure that policymakers are not relying on overstated extreme-event risks.

      Finally, if ERCOT elects to incorporate recency bias, it is unclear why weather years 2024 and
2025 have been omitted. ERCOT has indicated that portions of 2025 data may have availability
constraints; however, 2024 data is fully available and should be included to maintain methodological
consistency. Partial inclusion of 2025 data should also be considered if it is available as well.

7) ERCOT proposed using the multi-area reliability and economic dispatch modeling
   capability in SERVM to assess resource adequacy on a zonal basis that would account for
   transmission constraints between defined transmission zones. ERCOT states that any
   results from this analysis would be informational and not used to determine compliance
   with the reliability standard.
    a. Should the Commission approve an assessment of reliability metrics at the zonal level,
       understanding that these results would be purely informational and not used to
       determine compliance with the reliability standard?
    b. If so, do you have any proposed modifications to the approach ERCOT has
       recommended?

       ERCOT's proposal to conduct a zonal-level reliability assessment using the multiarea
modeling capabilities within SERVM may offer supplemental insight, but its application in this context
must be carefully qualified. The zonal analysis relies on dispatch assumptions and outage probabilities
that reflect average system conditions, which differ materially from the conditions present during
extreme events-the primary focus ofthis assessment. As a result, any zonal-level outputs would have
limited relevance to evaluating system performance under the high-stress reliability scenarios that
drive the Commission's reliability standard.

       Given these limitations, any zonal results should be explicitly characterized as informational
and should not be used for compliance purposes or interpreted as producing deterministic conclusions
regarding system adequacy. Moreover, several issues explored within this zonal construct are more
appropriately addressed through the ongoing Regional Transmission Plan ("RTP") process, rather than
through a resource-adequacy assessment designed to evaluate loss-of-load risk under extreme
conditions.

8)   ERCOT proposed modifying how the model accounts for the effectiveness of the
     Commission's weatherization rule 16 TAC § 25.55. Previously, it was estimated to reduce
     weather-related outages by 85%, however under ERCOT's proposed approach, the rule's
     effectiveness would decline during extreme temperatures.
      a. Do you agree with ERCOT's recommendation to deviate from the 85% effectiveness for
          the weatherization rule?

         Decreasing the assumed effectiveness of weatherization measures for temperatures below the
Commission-established standard may be reasonable in principle; however, the rate of degradation
proposed by ERCOT is excessively severe and unsupported by recent operational evidence. ERCOT's
methodology suggests that under conditions comparable to Winter Storm Uri, the substantial
 weatherization investments made over the past five years would provide no meaningful benefit,
despite extensive improvements across the generating fleet. This assumption is inconsistent with
observed generator performance and therefore lacks analytical justification.

        Recent weather events further demonstrate that ERCOT's proposed base line of only 85%
reduction of weather-related outages and erosion curve significantly understates generator capability.
During Winter Storm Fern, many areas experienced wind-chill conditions more than 10 degrees below
the weatherization standard without any correlated deterioration in weatherization effectiveness, and
most generators continued to operate reliably well below the required threshold. These data points
directly contradict the premise that benefits should disappear within a 15-degree temperature
differential.

     Given the magnitude ofthe potential impacts, adjusting this assumption is critically important.
ERCOT's initial trial analysis indicates that reducing weatherization effectiveness in the manner
proposed would nearly double the proj ected Loss of Load Expectation and magnitude in the 2026
assessment, with even more pronounced effects anticipated in the higher-load 2029 study year. Such
distortions would materially diminish the reliability and credibility of the study results.

        Accordingly, ERCOT should modify its baseline to incorporate evidence of overperformance
in the past storms and the proposed erosion curve methodology should either be removed or
significantly modified to reflect a more realistic, gradual decline in effectiveness, one that is consistent
with empirical performance data and the substantial weatherization efforts undertaken by the
generation community.

9) ERCOT has proposed assumptions for the outages:
    a. Are the assumptions for generation and ESR outage modeling reasonable? If not, what
        modifications do you propose?
    b. How should ERCOT treat planned transmission outages in the model?

        Transmission outages could only be taken into consideration in the zonal analysis and as
stated above that has limited value.

10) Please provide comments and recommendations on any of the model input assumptions that
   Staff has not specifically ilagged in previous questions.

        ERCOT's analysis of load-forecast error in the 2025 Ancillary Services (AS) methodology
found that historical load growth exhibited weak or inconsistent relationships with forecast-error
magnitudes, and therefore error inputs were not scaled with load levels. In contrast, the current study
applies fixed percentage error values, 0%, 2%, and 4%, which necessarily scale with total load and
disproportionately affect extreme-weather scenarios. This approach is inconsistent with ERCOT's
prior findings and results in an inflated representation of uncertainty, particularly given that the
underlying load forecast is already subject to considerable variability and appears likely to be
overstated in magnitude.

        Moreover, while forecast uncertainty may reasonably increase for later years, the assessment
does not apply a comparable uncertainty range to resource additions, creating an analytical imbalance
 between load- and supply-side assumptions. To maintain consistency and avoid compounding
conservatism, ERCOT should refrain from applying non-weather-based load-forecast error for the
2029 study year or, at a minimum, should employ the 2026 error probabilities instead.

        When conducting long-term projections of this nature, uncertainty is unavoidable. Providing a
broader range of scenarios and sensitivities, similar to the approach used in the CDR report, would
offer the Commission a more complete picture of potential outcomes. Additional efforts examining
adjustments to Ancillary Service Demand Curves ("ASDC"s) and increases to the system-wide offer
cap would further support evaluation of market-design options intended to incentivize the
development of additional dispatchable generation.

III.   Conclusion

        Shell Energy appreciates the Commission's thoughtful engagement on the assumptions guiding
the 2026 Reliability Assessment and welcomes the opportunity to contribute to this important process.
Ensuring that the study's inputs are accurate, transparent, and reflective of realistic system conditions
is essential to producing results that can meaningfully inform long-term market design and policy
decisions. Shell Energy respectfully submits the recommendations provided herein to support a more
credible, analytically sound assessment, and one that provides policymakers with the clarity necessary
to evaluate reliability outcomes and prioritize future market design considerations.

        Shell Energy remains fully available to discuss these comments in greater detail and to support
Staff or Commissioners with any additional analysis, clarification, or follow-up that may assist in the
development of a robust and reliable final assessment.

                                              IV.    Executive Summary
1. The reliability assessment must be grounded in accurate, evidence-based assumptions.
   Load credibility of the study depends on inputs that reflect realistic system conditions rather than conservative
   assumptions that inflate risk or distort outcomes.
2. An updated load forecast is essential to maintaining analytical integrity.
   The ERCOT's current forecasts produce implausibly high net-load levels, such as winter 2026 net loads
   exceeding 90 GW, which artificially increase modeled load-shed events. Aligning the assessment with the criteria
   in Project No. 58480, without grandfathering prior inclusions, is necessary even if it delays the study by a month.
3. The Cost of New Entry (CONE) must be updated to rellect actual development costs.
   The approved value of $140,000/MW-year is materially understated relative to the cost of new thermal resources.
   If retained, it would fail to reflect needed realistic investment signals, impede development of new dispatchable
   generation, and risk premature retirements.
4. Weatherization-effectiveness assumptions must rellect empirical performance.
   ERCOT should modify its baseline to incorporate evidence of overperformance in the past storms. ERCOT's
   proposed erosion curve eliminates weatherization benefits too quickly and should include a more gradual,
   evidence-based decline consistent with observed generator performance to avoid overstating loss-of-load risks.
5. Weather-year weighting must not inllate extreme-event probabilities.
   ERCOT's methodology increases the modeled probability ofWinter Storm Uri beyond its climatological range,
   biasing reliability results. More realistic probability assumptions should be used or at least studied as sensitivity
   for 2021 and 1989. Inclusion of 2024 and partial 2025 data is needed based on arguments for recency weighting.
6. Resource portfolio assumptions for 2029 must rellect heightened uncertainty.
   While the December 2025 CDR mix is reasonable for 2026, applying it to 2029 is inappropriate. ERCOT should
   include all Texas Energy Fund resources and apply PGRR 127's structured criteria to incorporate additional
   proj ects reasonably expected to enter service.
7. Magnitude thresholds must correspond to extreme-event conditions and based on all TDSP's abilities.
   ERCOT's proposed thresholds are based on moderate load and understate potential rotatable load. More realistic
   scaling indicates thresholds closer to 16 GW Increasing the number of rotational groups from two to three or four
   would further expand feasible rotatable load. The total load shed should not be calculated by using the lowest load
   rotation percentage from all TDSPs. Larger classes of TDSPs should have higher percentages, at a minimum.
8. Load curtailment under SB 6 should be treated as available tools in magnitude and duration calculations.
   The objective of curtailment options in SB6 is to maintain reliability during extreme events and hence those loads
   should be treated as curtailable rather than firm in magnitude and duration calculations.
9. Duplicate cases for 2021 and 1989 must not skew magnitude and duration calculation.
   Including duplicate scenarios skews empirical distributions and inflates results unless duplicates are excluded.
   This happens because: (1) magnitude and duration metrics rely on the empirical 99th percentile without
   probability weighting; (2) the added severe winter profiles disproportionately impact extreme violation counts.
   While more cases increase the number trimmed by the 1% threshold, doubling extreme cases offsets any
   reduction in skewness.
10. Load-forecast error should not scale with total load.
    ERCOT's prior analysis found no consistent relationship between load growth and forecast error, yet the current
    assessment applies percentage-based error rates that inflate uncertainty during extreme conditions.
11. Non-weather-based load-forecast error should not be applied to extreme years.
    The precise 2021 load, excluding firm load shed, remains unknown, and ERCOT's estimate appears to be
   overstated. Incorporating non-weather-related load forecast errors would further distort upwards already
   exaggerated winter storm Uri load data and significantly skew the result.
